The disturbing-frequency row is the one that separates a mount from a packing piece. A pad selected purely on load can sit close to the frequency it was meant to isolate and make the vibration worse; asking the question is how a supplier avoids delivering a technically correct part that fails its actual purpose.

🛑 Creep is the row that matters most and it exists on no page in the catalogue. Compression set measures what happens after a load is removed; creep measures what happens while it stays on, and a support pad is under load for the life of the vehicle or machine. It is the reason a body sits lower at five years than at one.

fields.label: Wrong default, and a missing option
paragraphs: 🛑 Natural rubber is not offered, and it is the compound engine mounts, body mounts and machine mounts are made from. Best fatigue resistance and highest resilience of the eight Margo mixes — and a pad that is loaded and unloaded for a decade is a fatigue problem before it is anything else.
🛑 EPDM is pre-selected. It weathers well and it creeps more than natural rubber under sustained load. On a support pad the default should follow the duty rather than the weather.
Margo produces every part in every compound it mixes (client-instructed 2026-09-02). Nothing is removed — all eight are ranked, and the four missing from the live selector are added.

fields.label: Selector
rows: The classic mounting compound. Best fatigue resistance and highest resilience of the eight, so it survives repeated loading and returns to height. Not for oil, and it perishes in prolonged sunlight
Where the pad is exposed to weather or sees oil. Good fatigue life, moderate oil resistance, better ozone resistance than natural rubber. The usual choice under a vehicle
Low-cost indoor and enclosed load pads. Fatigue life below natural rubber and no oil resistance
Weather, ozone and steam. Creeps more than natural rubber under sustained load, so allow for it in the deflection
Where the pad sits in oil. Poor ozone resistance, so not for an exposed position
High temperature. Low tear strength and poor fatigue resistance make it a weak choice under load
2–3× the cost and no fatigue advantage. Specify only where the medium demands it

fields.label: Cards ×4
rows: Hardness will not tell you how it behaves

Rubber cannot be compressed in volume, only bulged sideways — so a thin wide pad is far stiffer than a thick narrow one of the same compound and hardness. Send us the load and the deflection you can allow, and we will set the shape and the hardness together.
It keeps sinking after you fit it

Rubber under permanent load creeps for years. We allow for it at the design stage rather than shipping a pad that meets its deflection on day one and sits 2 mm lower at year five, closing your clearances.
Natural rubber, unless the position rules it out

It has the best fatigue resistance we mix, which is why mounts are made from it. Where the pad is exposed or sees oil we move to neoprene and say why — the trade is fatigue life against weathering, and it should be a decision, not a default.
Bonded inserts, moulded in one piece
Most mounting pads need a steel plate or a bolt sleeve. We bond rubber to metal in-house, so the insert is moulded in rather than fitted afterwards, and there is no joint to work loose.
fields.note:
Four cards, four cards — no count change and no new element.
Card 01 is the strongest technical argument available on any page in this set, because it corrects a belief most buyers hold — that hardness is the specification — and it does so in two sentences.
Card 04 sells a capability Margo has and never mentions. Rubber-to-metal bonding is client-confirmed, it is what makes a real mounting pad possible, and it appears nowhere on the live site

sections.title: From compound to certification
sections.chip: Bonding and load testing are missing steps
sections.live: LIVE H2 → From Compound to Certification · six steps · the same text as all 31 pages

fields.label: Steps
rows: Material compounding — polymer blending, additive integration and batch QC in our in-house lab. The compound is chosen for fatigue life first on a load-bearing part.
Mould design and CNC tool manufacture, in-house, held as a controlled record. Footprint and thickness are set together to reach the spring rate, since both govern how stiff the pad behaves.
Compression moulding, with any steel insert bonded to the rubber in the same operation.
Post-cure and trimming, and a bond check on inserted pads.
Quality inspection — dimensional check, hardness, and load-deflection tested on batch samples against the approved drawing.
Export packaging — industrial packing with documentation. Pads are packed unloaded, since rubber stored under compression takes a set. ISPM-15 treated pallets where timber is used.
fields.note:
Six steps, six kept. The live text says “ISO-certified lab” in step 01, which becomes “in-house lab”; step 03 says “Compression Moulding” alone and gains the bonding operation; step 04 is “Post-Cure & Trimming” and gains the bond check.
Step 05 is the one that makes the page credible. Load-deflection testing on batch samples is what turns the spring rate from a claim into a controlled characteristic — and it is the check an OEM will ask about.
Step 02 states the shape-factor argument as a production fact rather than a marketing line

notes: The process block must render from the part record.

sections.title: Certified to international standards
sections.chip: 🛑 EN 1337 is the misreading to close off
sections.live: LIVE H2 → Certified to International Standards · ISO 9001 only — honest

fields.label: Credit, an addition, a caution
paragraphs: ISO 9001:2015 claimed and nothing else — no IATF, no TÜV SÜD, no CE marking. The production table prints “On request” rather than inventing figures, and the video says “Film pending”. The scope covers a moulded pad, so the badge stands unqualified.

🛑 The specific risk on this page is structural bearings. A rubber load pad is visually indistinguishable from an elastomeric bridge or building bearing, and those are certified products under EN 1337 with CE marking and third-party surveillance. Margo holds none of it. An unqualified “certified to international standards” heading beside a load-bearing pad invites exactly that enquiry.
Add the client-instructed IATF line (2026-08-31): upgrading to IATF 16949, targeted end 2026; ISO 14001 and 45001 targeted 2027 — stated as a plan, never as held.
